Smart home standard Matter 1.5 adds cameras and energy reporting

Published 2026-10-07 13:30 UTC

The Connectivity Standards Alliance has published Matter 1.5, and the headline addition is one that smart home owners have been asking about since the standard launched: cameras. Until now, Matter covered lights, locks, plugs, thermostats and sensors, but video doorbells and security cameras still needed each manufacturer's own app and cloud account.

Matter 1.5 defines a camera device type that supports live streaming over WebRTC, two-way audio, pan and tilt controls, and privacy zones that blank out parts of the frame. Recording is left to the controller, so a hub from one company can store clips from a camera made by another. The alliance says streams stay on the local network unless the user opts into remote viewing.

The second big change is energy reporting. Plugs, appliances and heat pumps can now publish how much power they draw in real time and how much energy they used over a day. Controllers can combine those readings into a household dashboard, and utilities that run demand-response programs can ask compatible devices to shift their consumption to cheaper hours.

Manufacturers will need firmware updates before any of this reaches homes. Several hub makers told Ars they expect to ship Matter 1.5 support in the first half of next year, and camera makers said certification testing for the new device type opens in December. Existing Matter devices keep working without changes.

The update also tidies up multi-admin setups, where one device is controlled by several ecosystems at once. Matter 1.5 adds a way for a device to tell every connected controller when its name or room assignment changes, which should end the confusing situation where a lamp is called one thing in one app and something else in another.

Critics note that Matter's slow rollout has frustrated buyers who were promised that any device would work with any hub. The alliance acknowledges the gap and says the camera spec took longer than planned because members disagreed about how much video processing should happen on the device itself.
